title: High Blood Pressure After Drinking: Why It Spikes the Next Day
excerpt: Why blood pressure often reads high the morning after drinking, how long the spike lasts, how to bring it down safely, and the readings that mean you should get help.
metaDescription: Why blood pressure reads high the day after drinking, how long it lasts, how to lower it safely, and which readings mean you should see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** it's common for blood pressure to read higher than usual the morning after a night of drinking, and for most healthy social drinkers it's a temporary rebound that settles within about a day. Alcohol first relaxes your blood vessels, so blood pressure can dip for a few hours. Then, as your body clears the alcohol, your nervous system and stress hormones push the other way, and a short night, dehydration, salty food, and extra coffee add to it. That said, a reading that's very high, or comes with chest pain, a severe headache, or trouble speaking, is not a hangover symptom to sleep off. This guide explains why the spike happens, what numbers matter, how to bring it down sensibly, and when to get help.

> **When to see a doctor or call 911.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 right away** if your blood pressure is 180/120 or higher *and* you have chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness or weakness in your face, arm, or leg, a change in vision, difficulty speaking, sudden confusion, or the worst headache of your life. **Contact your doctor promptly** if you get 180/120 or higher on two readings five minutes apart without symptoms, if your heart is racing or beating irregularly and doesn't settle, or if you take blood pressure medication and your readings are often high after drinking. **Get medical help the same day** if you drink heavily every day and, after stopping or cutting back, you have high blood pressure along with shaking, sweating, a fast pulse, or feel very agitated. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous and is treatable.

## Why Blood Pressure Goes Up After Drinking

Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. It's written as two numbers: the top (systolic) number is the pressure when your heart beats, and the bottom (diastolic) number is the pressure between beats. Both can move a lot through the day in response to stress, sleep, food, and activity. Alcohol nudges almost every one of those levers.

### The first few hours: a dip

Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes and widens blood vessels. That's why your face can flush and you feel warm after a drink or two. Wider vessels mean less resistance, so blood pressure often falls a little in the first few hours after drinking. Your heart usually speeds up slightly at the same time to compensate.

### The next morning: the rebound

As your liver clears the alcohol, the picture flips. Your body has been working against the alcohol's relaxing effect all evening, and when the alcohol is gone those counter-forces are briefly left unopposed. Several things happen together:

- **Your sympathetic nervous system revs up.** This is the "fight or flight" system that tightens blood vessels and speeds up your heart. Drinking activates it, and the activation tends to linger into the next day.
- **Stress hormones rise.** Alcohol increases cortisol and adrenaline-type hormones, both of which raise blood pressure.
- **Fluid-balancing hormones shift.** Alcohol suppresses the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more. Your body then responds to the fluid loss by activating hormones (part of what doctors call the renin-angiotensin system) that narrow blood vessels and retain salt.

This pattern has been seen in research, not just in anecdotes. A 2020 Cochrane review that pooled controlled studies of single drinking sessions found that after higher amounts of alcohol, blood pressure tended to fall over the first several hours and then rise above baseline roughly half a day later, while heart rate stayed elevated throughout. In everyday terms: drink a lot in the evening, and your reading the next morning or early afternoon is likely to be higher than your normal.

### The hangover amplifiers

The rebound is only part of the story. The morning after usually stacks several other blood-pressure raisers on top of it:

- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it fragments the second half of the night. Short or broken sleep raises blood pressure the next day on its own. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.
- **Dehydration.** Losing fluid makes your body squeeze its blood vessels to keep circulation steady. See [does alcohol dehydrate you?](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) for how much fluid alcohol actually costs you.
- **Salty food.** Late-night pizza, fries, and a greasy breakfast carry a lot of sodium, which pulls water into your bloodstream and raises pressure, especially in people who are salt-sensitive.
- **Extra caffeine.** Coffee and energy drinks can raise blood pressure for a few hours, particularly in people who don't drink them every day.
- **Hangover medicines.** Ibuprofen and naproxen can raise blood pressure, and decongestants such as pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine (common in cold and sinus products) narrow blood vessels.
- **Pain, nausea, and anxiety.** A pounding headache and that anxious, on-edge hangover feeling both trigger the same stress response that pushes your numbers up.
- **Nicotine.** If you smoked or vaped more than usual, nicotine tightens blood vessels and raises blood pressure.

Put all of that together and it's easy to see why a cuff reading the morning after can look alarming even in someone whose blood pressure is normally fine.

## Does Alcohol Raise Blood Pressure the Next Day?

Yes, it often does, especially after more than two or three drinks. The more you drink in one sitting, the more likely you are to see a next-day rise, and the larger it tends to be. One or two drinks with dinner are less likely to cause a noticeable spike for most people, and some will see their blood pressure slightly lower that evening.

How large the rise is varies widely. It depends on how much you drank, how fast, whether you ate, how well you slept, your age, your genes, and whether you already have high blood pressure. People who already have hypertension, or who are on the edge of it, often see bigger swings. That's one reason doctors ask how much you drink when they're working out why someone's blood pressure is hard to control.

It's also worth knowing that the effect works in both directions over time. When regular drinkers cut back, blood pressure usually comes down. A widely cited 2017 meta-analysis in *The Lancet Public Health* found that reducing alcohol lowered blood pressure in people who had been drinking more than about two drinks a day, with the biggest benefit in the heaviest drinkers. Alcohol is one of the more reversible causes of high blood pressure.

## How Long Does Blood Pressure Stay High After Drinking?

For most social drinkers, a next-day rise settles within about 24 hours, once the alcohol is fully cleared and you've slept, eaten, and rehydrated. After a very heavy session or a run of several nights out, readings can stay a bit elevated for longer while your sleep and stress hormones get back to normal.

A useful rule of thumb:

- **High the morning after, normal two days later:** most likely the temporary rebound described above.
- **Still high two or three days later with no drinking:** this suggests your baseline blood pressure may be higher than you think. Book a check with your doctor.
- **High most days, not just after drinking:** this is high blood pressure, whatever the cause, and it deserves proper evaluation. Regular drinking may be part of the reason, but it needs a doctor's input.

## What Counts as High? Understanding Your Numbers

US guidelines from the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology group adult blood pressure readings like this:

| Category | Top number (systolic) | And/or | Bottom number (diastolic) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | Less than 120 | and | Less than 80 |
| Elevated | 120 to 129 | and | Less than 80 |
| High blood pressure, stage 1 | 130 to 139 | or | 80 to 89 |
| High blood pressure, stage 2 | 140 or higher | or | 90 or higher |
| Severe (hypertensive crisis range) | Higher than 180 | and/or | Higher than 120 |

Two things matter here. First, **one reading is not a diagnosis.** High blood pressure is diagnosed from repeated readings on different days, ideally including home or ambulatory monitoring. A single high number the morning after drinking tells you that your blood pressure was high at that moment, not that you have hypertension. Second, **the severe range is the one to act on immediately**, as described in the box above.

## Is It Dangerous? When a Spike Matters

For a healthy adult, a temporary bump into the 130s or 140s the morning after a night out is unlikely to cause harm by itself. Your blood vessels handle short swings every day, for example when you climb stairs or get stressed in traffic.

It matters more in a few situations:

- **You already have high blood pressure, heart disease, or kidney disease.** Spikes stack on top of an already raised baseline.
- **You have had a stroke, a TIA (mini-stroke), or an aneurysm,** or a doctor has told you to keep your blood pressure tightly controlled.
- **You're pregnant.** High blood pressure in pregnancy always needs prompt medical attention, and alcohol isn't recommended in pregnancy.
- **Your heart rhythm feels irregular.** Heavy drinking sessions can trigger atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, even in people with no heart history. Doctors sometimes call this "holiday heart." If your pulse feels chaotic, fluttering, or very fast and doesn't settle with rest, get checked. Our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers this in more detail.
- **The spikes are getting bigger or more frequent.** That's a sign the drinking pattern is affecting your cardiovascular system and is worth discussing with a doctor.

### Signs that point to an emergency, not a hangover

Some symptoms overlap with a bad hangover, which makes it easy to dismiss them. Don't. Call 911 if you have very high blood pressure together with any of these, or any of these on their own and suddenly:

- Chest pain, pressure, or tightness
- Shortness of breath
- Sudden severe headache, unlike your usual hangover headache
- Numbness or weakness on one side of the face or body, a drooping face, or slurred or confused speech (signs of a stroke)
- Sudden blurred or lost vision
- Severe back pain
- Confusion, extreme drowsiness, or a seizure

### High blood pressure and alcohol withdrawal

This section matters for a specific group: people who drink heavily most days. If you fall into that group and you stop suddenly or cut back sharply, high blood pressure can be part of alcohol withdrawal, along with shaking hands, sweating, a fast heartbeat, nausea, anxiety, and trouble sleeping. Withdrawal can escalate to seizures or confusion, which is a medical emergency. If this sounds like what you're experiencing, contact a doctor or urgent care the same day, and call 911 for confusion, hallucinations, or a seizure. Doctors can manage withdrawal safely. This is very different from the ordinary next-day rebound most social drinkers notice, but it's important to know the difference.

## How to Bring Your Blood Pressure Down After Drinking

For a typical next-day rise without warning symptoms, the goal is to remove the things pushing your numbers up and let your body settle. None of these are dramatic, but together they help.

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water through the morning rather than chugging a liter at once. If you lost fluid through vomiting or diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink can help. Note that these contain sodium; that's useful for rehydration, but if your doctor has put you on a low-salt diet, check the label and don't overdo them. Our [electrolytes and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains when they're worth it.
2. **Eat a real meal, lighter on salt.** Choose something like eggs, oatmeal, yogurt, bananas, potatoes, or leafy greens. Potassium-rich foods help balance sodium. Skip the heavily salted fast-food breakfast if you can.
3. **Go easy on caffeine.** One normal cup of coffee is fine for most people. Three cups or an energy drink on a hangover is likely to push both your blood pressure and your heart rate higher.
4. **Rest, and nap if you can.** Making up some lost sleep helps your stress hormones come back down.
5. **Take a gentle walk.** Light activity and fresh air can help you feel better and support normal blood pressure later in the day. Save hard workouts for when you feel fully recovered.
6. **Breathe slowly.** A few minutes of slow, deep breathing (for example, in for four seconds, out for six) calms the fight-or-flight response that's driving part of the spike.
7. **Be choosy with hangover medicine.** If you have high blood pressure or take medication for it, avoid decongestants and ask a pharmacist before using ibuprofen or naproxen. Acetaminophen doesn't usually raise blood pressure, but it carries its own liver warning for people who drink. Read our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before reaching for it.
8. **Don't drink more to feel better.** The "hair of the dog" just restarts the cycle and pushes the rebound later.
9. **Re-check later, properly.** Measure again in the afternoon or the next morning once you've recovered, using the method below.

### What not to do

- **Don't take extra blood pressure medication** or someone else's pills to bring the number down. Taking more than prescribed can drop your blood pressure too far and cause dizziness or fainting.
- **Don't skip your regular blood pressure medication** because you drank. If you're unsure whether your medicine is safe with alcohol, ask your pharmacist.
- **Don't rely on a supplement or "detox" product** to lower blood pressure. There is no good evidence that any hangover supplement does this.

## How to Measure Your Blood Pressure Accurately

A lot of alarming morning-after readings come from measuring the wrong way. A hurried reading taken while you're anxious, dehydrated, and on your second coffee can read noticeably higher than your real number. To get a reading you can trust:

- **Use a validated upper-arm cuff** in the right size for your arm. Wrist and finger devices are less reliable. In the US, the AMA-backed list at validatebp.org shows which home monitors have been checked for accuracy.
- **Wait 30 minutes after caffeine, exercise, or smoking,** and empty your bladder first.
- **Sit quietly for five minutes** with your back supported and feet flat on the floor, legs uncrossed.
- **Rest your arm on a table** so the cuff sits at heart level, on bare skin rather than over a sleeve.
- **Don't talk** during the reading.
- **Take two or three readings a minute apart** and note the average.

If you want to know how drinking affects you personally, a simple experiment helps: take readings for a week of normal mornings without alcohol, then compare them with the mornings after you drink. Bring the log to your doctor. It's far more useful to them than a single scary number.

## Blood Pressure Medication and Alcohol

If you already take medicine for high blood pressure, alcohol affects you in two ways.

**In the short term,** alcohol's relaxing effect on blood vessels can add to the effect of some blood pressure medicines, so you may feel dizzy or lightheaded, especially when standing up quickly. This is particularly noted with alpha-blockers and some other drugs that relax blood vessels. Standing up slowly and staying hydrated helps, but if you feel faint, sit or lie down and tell your doctor about it.

**Over the longer term,** regular heavier drinking can push your blood pressure up and make your medicine look like it isn't working. Doctors often check alcohol intake when blood pressure stays high despite treatment.

Every medicine is different, so the safest step is a short conversation with your pharmacist or doctor about how much alcohol, if any, is sensible with your specific prescriptions. Our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) covers the most common interactions.

## Is It Safe to Drink If You Have High Blood Pressure?

That's a decision to make with your doctor, because it depends on how high your blood pressure is, what other conditions you have, and what you take. General US guidance says that adults who drink should keep it to no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women, and blood pressure guidelines recommend people with hypertension stay within those limits or lower. A standard drink in the US is about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits.

Patterns matter as well as totals. Five drinks on Saturday is harder on your blood pressure than the same five spread across a week, because the rebound effect scales with how much you drink in one sitting. If you notice clear spikes after nights out, that's useful information: it's your body showing you its threshold.

Practical habits that help:

- Eat before and while you drink.
- Alternate each alcoholic drink with a glass of water.
- Set a limit before you go out and pace yourself to roughly one drink an hour or slower.
- Watch the salty bar snacks.
- Keep some nights alcohol-free each week.
- Protect your sleep after a night out.

For a deeper dive into the long-term relationship, see our guide to [alcohol and high blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) and our broader look at [alcohol and heart health](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-heart-health-complete-cardiovascular-guide-2025).

## Low Blood Pressure After Drinking

Not everyone sees a high reading. Some people feel dizzy and lightheaded and find their blood pressure is *lower* than usual, especially the evening of drinking or early the next morning. That's the vasodilation effect plus dehydration. It's more common if you didn't eat, lost fluid through vomiting, take blood pressure medicine, or stood up quickly. Sit or lie down, drink fluids, and stand up slowly. If you faint, feel confused, have chest pain, or the dizziness doesn't improve as you rehydrate, get medical help.

## Can Anything Prevent the Spike?

The most reliable way to avoid a next-day blood pressure rise is to drink less in one sitting. Beyond that, the habits that reduce hangovers in general also take some of the pressure off: eating, pacing, hydrating, and sleeping enough. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the steps with the best evidence.

Some people also use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, on nights they drink. It's worth being clear about what it does and doesn't do. DHM's research is mostly about how the body handles alcohol and about hangover symptoms, and most of it comes from animal studies with limited human data. **There is no good evidence that DHM lowers blood pressure or prevents a post-drinking spike,** and it is not a treatment for hypertension. If you're interested in it for hangovers, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take blood pressure medication or other prescriptions, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is a good starting point.

## The Bottom Line

A higher-than-usual blood pressure reading the morning after drinking is common. It comes from alcohol's rebound effect on your blood vessels, nervous system, and hormones, made worse by poor sleep, dehydration, salt, caffeine, and some hangover medicines. For most social drinkers it fades within a day with water, food, rest, and patience.

Take it seriously when the reading is 180/120 or higher, when it comes with chest pain, breathing trouble, stroke signs, or an irregular heartbeat, when it stays high for days, or when you take blood pressure medicine. And if you regularly see spikes after drinking, treat that as a useful early signal: cutting back is one of the most effective ways to bring blood pressure down.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why is my blood pressure high the day after drinking?**

After a bigger night, blood pressure often dips for the first few hours while alcohol widens your blood vessels, then climbs above your normal level as the alcohol wears off. Your stress hormones and nervous system rev up during that rebound, and dehydration, short or broken sleep, salty food, extra coffee, and some hangover painkillers can all push the number higher. For most social drinkers this is temporary and settles within a day or so.

**How long does blood pressure stay high after drinking?**

For most people, a next-day rise settles within roughly 24 hours once they have slept, eaten, and rehydrated, though a very heavy session can leave readings elevated a little longer. Research on single drinking sessions has found blood pressure tends to rise above baseline about half a day after higher amounts of alcohol. If your readings are still high two or three days later, or they are high most of the time, that points to an underlying blood pressure problem worth checking with a doctor.

**What blood pressure reading after drinking is an emergency?**

A reading of 180/120 or higher together with symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness or weakness, a change in vision, trouble speaking, or confusion is an emergency. Call 911. If you get 180/120 or higher with no symptoms, sit quietly for five minutes and measure again. If it is still that high, contact your doctor right away.

**Does alcohol raise or lower blood pressure?**

Both, depending on the dose and the timing. A drink or two can lower blood pressure slightly for a few hours because alcohol relaxes blood vessels. Larger amounts tend to cause a dip followed by a rise above normal later. Over months and years, regular drinking above moderate levels is one of the more common, and more reversible, causes of high blood pressure.

**Should I check my blood pressure when I'm hungover?**

You can, but treat the number as a snapshot of a stressed body, not your true baseline. Hangover readings are often skewed by dehydration, poor sleep, caffeine, and a racing heart. If you want to know your real blood pressure, measure on several ordinary mornings when you have not been drinking, using a validated upper-arm cuff and the same routine each time.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover if my blood pressure is high?**

Be cautious. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can raise blood pressure and can blunt the effect of some blood pressure medicines, and they are also hard on a stomach already irritated by alcohol. If you have high blood pressure or take medication for it, ask a pharmacist or doctor which pain reliever suits you. Also avoid decongestants such as pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine unless your doctor has okayed them.

**Is it safe to drink if I have high blood pressure?**

Many people with high blood pressure are told by their doctor that light drinking is acceptable, while others are advised to cut back or stop. US guidance for people who drink suggests no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women, and for people with hypertension, less is generally better. Alcohol can also interact with blood pressure medicines, so ask your doctor what is right for you.

**Does DHM lower blood pressure?**

There is no good evidence that DHM lowers blood pressure in people or protects against a post-drinking spike. DHM's research is mainly about alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. It is not a treatment for high blood pressure and should not replace any medication or medical advice.
